question: What is the primary definition of pharmacology?

options.A: The study of how drugs interact with living systems
options.B: The physical examination of pregnant women
options.C: The manufacturing process of herbal remedies
options.D: The study of disease outbreaks in communities

explanation: Pharmacology specifically examines the interactions between chemical substances and living organisms to produce therapeutic effects. [learn more](BMP124_U1_T1#BMP124_U1_T1_h1)

question: Why must midwives have a solid understanding of pharmacology during pregnancy?

options.A: Medications given to a mother can cross over to affect the baby
options.B: It helps midwives diagnose rare tropical diseases independently
options.C: Pregnant women metabolize all medications at the exact same rate
options.D: Midwives are solely responsible for manufacturing hospital drugs

explanation: Most drugs administered during pregnancy cross the placenta, meaning the midwife is treating two distinct individuals simultaneously. [learn more](BMP124_U1_T1#BMP124_U1_T1_h1)

question: Which branch of pharmacology studies what the body does to a drug?

options.A: Toxicology
options.B: Pharmacokinetics
options.C: Pharmacodynamics
options.D: Pharmaceutics

explanation: Pharmacokinetics covers the movement of drugs through the body, broken down into absorption, distribution, metabolism, and excretion. [learn more](BMP124_U1_T1#BMP124_U1_T1_h2)

question: What does the term pharmacodynamics refer to?

options.A: How the liver breaks down chemical waste
options.B: The manufacturing cost of essential medicines
options.C: How the drug affects the body's systems
options.D: The speed at which a pill dissolves in water

explanation: Pharmacodynamics focuses on the biological and physiological effects of drugs and their mechanisms of action. [learn more](BMP124_U1_T1#BMP124_U1_T1_h2)

question: What is the function of a drug receptor in the body?

options.A: To store excess vitamins inside bone marrow cells
options.B: To filter waste products directly out of the bloodstream
options.C: To bind with specific drug molecules and trigger a response
options.D: To manufacture natural hormones during labor

explanation: Receptors are specialized cellular sites where drug molecules attach to initiate their specific biochemical effects. [learn more](BMP124_U1_T1#BMP124_U1_T1_h3)

question: How does a drug classified as an agonist work?

options.A: It speeds up the renal excretion of toxic waste
options.B: It blocks a receptor to stop any chemical activity
options.C: It destroys excess white blood cells in the spleen
options.D: It binds to a receptor and activates a bodily response

explanation: Agonists mimic the body's natural signaling chemicals by binding to receptors and turning on specific cellular functions. [learn more](BMP124_U1_T1#BMP124_U1_T1_h3)

question: What does the letter 'M' stand for in the ADME acronym of pharmacokinetics?

options.A: Movement
options.B: Metabolism
options.C: Monitoring
options.D: Malformation

explanation: In pharmacokinetics, metabolism refers to the chemical breakdown or alteration of drugs by the body, mainly in the liver. [learn more](BMP124_U1_T1#BMP124_U1_T1_h4)

question: Where does the primary excretion of most drug metabolites occur in the human body?

options.A: Skin
options.B: Kidneys
options.C: Lungs
options.D: Stomach

explanation: The kidneys filter blood and eliminate the majority of drugs and their breakdown products through urine. [learn more](BMP124_U1_T1#BMP124_U1_T1_h4)

question: Which physiological change during pregnancy directly affects how the body processes medications?

options.A: Increased blood volume and altered kidney filtration
options.B: The total elimination of gastric acid production
options.C: A complete shutdown of all liver enzyme functions
options.D: Decreased heart rate throughout all three trimesters

explanation: Pregnancy causes major hemodynamic shifts, including higher blood volume and changes in renal clearance, which alter drug distribution and elimination. [learn more](BMP124_U1_T1#BMP124_U1_T1_h5)

question: What is the most important clinical consideration for a midwife before administering any drug to an expectant mother?

options.A: Waiting until the postnatal period to provide any treatment
options.B: Ensuring the drug is manufactured exclusively within Nigeria
options.C: Weighing the therapeutic benefits against potential risks to the foetus
options.D: Confirming that the patient has never taken a tablet before

explanation: Because drugs cross the placenta, midwives must carefully balance the clinical need of the mother against potential harm to the baby. [learn more](BMP124_U1_T1#BMP124_U1_T1_h5)

question: Why do healthcare workers use a standard system for naming medicines?

options.A: To help patients memorize foreign languages
options.B: To make drug manufacturing more expensive
options.C: To ensure clear communication among health workers
options.D: To hide the true chemical makeup of a medicine

explanation: A standardized naming system allows midwives, doctors, and pharmacists to discuss treatments accurately without confusion. [learn more](BMP124_U1_T2#BMP124_U1_T2_h1)

question: Why do most medicines have more than one name?

options.A: Midwives prefer using complex chemical terms only
options.B: Local herbs do not have official scientific titles
options.C: The government changes the name every single year
options.D: Different companies and scientists use different naming systems

explanation: A single medicine often gets a chemical description, an official non-proprietary name, and various brand names depending on the manufacturer. [learn more](BMP124_U1_T2#BMP124_U1_T2_h1)

question: What does a drug's chemical name tell you about it?

options.A: The commercial price set by the pharmacy
options.B: The country where the drug was manufactured
options.C: Which disease the medicine treats best
options.D: Its exact atomic and molecular structure

explanation: Chemical names spell out the precise chemical building blocks and arrangement of atoms within the drug molecule. [learn more](BMP124_U1_T2#BMP124_U1_T2_h2)

question: Why do midwives avoid using chemical names during daily ward rounds?

options.A: The Nursing and Midwifery Council forbids speaking chemistry
options.B: Patients refuse to take drugs with chemical titles
options.C: Chemical names only apply to traditional herbal remedies
options.D: They are far too long and complicated to speak easily

explanation: Because chemical names describe complex molecular structures, they are impractical for fast-paced clinical communication and prescription writing. [learn more](BMP124_U1_T2#BMP124_U1_T2_h2)

question: Who usually assigns the official generic name to a new drug?

options.A: Patient advocacy groups in local communities
options.B: The local patent office in each individual state
options.C: International bodies like the World Health Organization
options.D: Private manufacturing companies seeking profit

explanation: Global organizations coordinate to give drugs clear, non-proprietary generic names that remain consistent worldwide. [learn more](BMP124_U1_T2#BMP124_U1_T2_h3)

question: How does knowing drug name endings (stems) help a midwife in practice?

options.A: It helps identify the drug class and general function quickly
options.B: It tells the exact financial cost of the medication
options.C: It guarantees the medication will be completely free of side effects
options.D: It allows the midwife to manufacture the drug at home

explanation: Recognizing common suffixes lets clinicians deduce how an unfamiliar drug works based on its generic name ending. [learn more](BMP124_U1_T2#BMP124_U1_T2_h3)

question: What is another common term for a proprietary drug name?

options.A: Chemical formula
options.B: Brand name
options.C: Molecular title
options.D: Generic stem

explanation: Proprietary names are commercial brand names created and registered by individual pharmaceutical companies. [learn more](BMP124_U1_T2#BMP124_U1_T2_h4)

question: Why might a single generic medicine be sold under many different brand names?

options.A: The chemical structure changes every time a new factory opens
options.B: Hospitals require a new brand name for every patient admitted
options.C: Multiple competing companies manufacture and market their own versions
options.D: Government regulations forbid using the same name twice

explanation: Once a drug's patent protection expires, various pharmaceutical firms can produce it and give it their own unique trade names. [learn more](BMP124_U1_T2#BMP124_U1_T2_h4)

question: Which type of drug name is controlled directly by the pharmaceutical company that makes it?

options.A: International non-proprietary name
options.B: Generic name
options.C: Proprietary name
options.D: Chemical name

explanation: Commercial manufacturers create and trademark proprietary names to market their specific products. [learn more](BMP124_U1_T2#BMP124_U1_T2_h5)

question: What should a midwife do when the hospital changes the brand of a commonly used drug?

options.A: Throw away all the old stock immediately without checking
options.B: Check the generic name to confirm the active ingredient is identical
options.C: Assume the new drug is completely unrelated and dangerous
options.D: Refuse to administer any medication that has a colorful wrapper

explanation: Looking at the generic name ensures the active drug substance is correct, regardless of what commercial brand name is printed on the new box. [learn more](BMP124_U1_T2#BMP124_U1_T2_h5)

question: What does the safety acronym LASA stand for in pharmacology?

options.A: Late antenatal screening assessment
options.B: Look-alike sound-alike
options.C: Local anesthetic safety audit
options.D: Large action systemic agent

explanation: LASA refers to drug names that are easily confused visually or verbally, which is a major cause of clinical medication errors. [learn more](BMP124_U1_T2#BMP124_U1_T2_h6)

question: How does tall-man lettering help prevent medication errors on the ward?

options.A: It uses capital letters to highlight the differing parts of similar drug names
options.B: It automatically calculates the correct dosage for pregnant women
options.C: It ensures that only senior doctors are allowed to write dangerous drugs
options.D: It prints prescription orders in giant fonts for nurses with poor eyesight

explanation: By capitalizing specific syllables in look-alike drug names, tall-man lettering draws the eye to what makes the two medications distinct. [learn more](BMP124_U1_T2#BMP124_U1_T2_h6)

question: Where do most medicines used in healthcare originally come from?

options.A: Extracted purely from synthetic petroleum
options.B: Derived only from marine microorganisms
options.C: Natural environments or laboratory synthesis
options.D: Synthesized exclusively in hospital pharmacies

explanation: Medications come from natural sources like plants and animals or are manufactured through laboratory processes. [learn more](BMP124_U1_T3#BMP124_U1_T3_h1)

question: Why is it helpful for a midwife to know where a prescribed drug comes from?

options.A: Laboratory-made drugs do not require any regulatory approval
options.B: Natural plant derivatives never cause allergic reactions in patients
options.C: It helps in understanding how substances are isolated and standardized
options.D: It guarantees the medication will be completely free of side effects

explanation: Knowing a drug's origin helps explain how it is prepared and standardized for safe clinical use. [learn more](BMP124_U1_T3#BMP124_U1_T3_h1)

question: Which plant part is the traditional source of quinine used to treat malaria?

options.A: Digitalis leaf blades
options.B: Nightshade seed pods
options.C: Opium poppy roots
options.D: Cinchona tree bark

explanation: Quinine is extracted from the bark of the Cinchona tree. [learn more](BMP124_U1_T3#BMP124_U1_T3_h2)

question: A patient is given a heart medication derived from the digitalis plant. What is this drug called?

options.A: Digoxin
options.B: Atropine
options.C: Quinine
options.D: Morphine

explanation: Digoxin is a cardiac medication obtained from the foxglove or digitalis plant. [learn more](BMP124_U1_T3#BMP124_U1_T3_h2)

question: Which animal organs were historically used to extract insulin before modern synthetic methods?

options.A: Pancreas of cattle and swine
options.B: Liver tissues of sheep and goats
options.C: Adrenal glands of poultry
options.D: Kidneys of equine species

explanation: Early insulin was extracted from the pancreatic glands of slaughtered cows and pigs. [learn more](BMP124_U1_T3#BMP124_U1_T3_h3)

question: What primary medical purpose did animal-derived heparin serve in clinical practice?

options.A: Lowering elevated blood glucose levels
options.B: Preventing abnormal blood clotting
options.C: Stimulating strong uterine contractions
options.D: Relieving acute postpartum pain

explanation: Heparin is an anticoagulant sourced from animal tissues that stops blood clots from forming. [learn more](BMP124_U1_T3#BMP124_U1_T3_h3)

question: Which mineral is critical in midwifery for managing severe pre-eclampsia and eclampsia?

options.A: Calcium carbonate
options.B: Ferrous sulfate
options.C: Magnesium sulfate
options.D: Sodium chloride

explanation: Magnesium sulfate is the standard medication used to prevent and control eclamptic seizures. [learn more](BMP124_U1_T3#BMP124_U1_T3_h4)

question: A pregnant woman attending antenatal care has low hemoglobin levels. Which mineral supplement is she most likely to receive?

options.A: Ferrous sulfate
options.B: Potassium chloride
options.C: Magnesium sulfate
options.D: Calcium carbonate

explanation: Iron supplements like ferrous sulfate are prescribed to prevent and treat anemia during pregnancy. [learn more](BMP124_U1_T3#BMP124_U1_T3_h4)

question: What is the main advantage of producing drugs through laboratory synthesis instead of relying only on plants?

options.A: Laboratory chemicals require zero quality control testing
options.B: They are guaranteed to never produce any adverse reactions
options.C: Reliable mass production independent of seasonal harvests
options.D: Natural plant extracts are entirely illegal to manufacture

explanation: Synthetic manufacturing allows continuous drug production without depending on seasonal crop yields. [learn more](BMP124_U1_T3#BMP124_U1_T3_h5)

question: Why do scientists often modify synthetic drug structures after discovering a successful chemical template?

options.A: To convert organic compounds strictly back into mineral salts
options.B: To eliminate the need for clinical trials entirely
options.C: To ensure the final product tastes sweet for pediatric patients
options.D: To improve potency and minimize unwanted side effects

explanation: Modifying chemical structures helps optimize how a drug works while reducing side effects. [learn more](BMP124_U1_T3#BMP124_U1_T3_h5)

question: Which living organisms are commonly used as host cells in biotechnology to manufacture human proteins?

options.A: Opium poppy plants
options.B: Marine algae spores
options.C: Cattle and swine
options.D: Bacteria or yeast

explanation: Microorganisms like bacteria and yeast are genetically altered to produce human proteins safely. [learn more](BMP124_U1_T3#BMP124_U1_T3_h6)

question: What is a major clinical benefit of using recombinant human insulin over animal-sourced insulin?

options.A: It can be extracted directly from wild forest plants
options.B: It does not require refrigeration under any circumstances
options.C: It is classified strictly as an inorganic mineral salt
options.D: It triggers fewer allergic and immune reactions in patients

explanation: Recombinant insulin matches human sequences, reducing immune complications sometimes seen with animal proteins. [learn more](BMP124_U1_T3#BMP124_U1_T3_h6)

question: Why must a midwife ask antenatal patients about their use of traditional herbal remedies?

options.A: Traditional roots and leaves are always chemically identical to synthetic pills
options.B: Herbal preparations contain active chemicals that can interact with prescribed drugs
options.C: Plant extracts cannot cross the placental barrier into fetal circulation
options.D: Local herbs are legally required to be registered as mineral supplements

explanation: Herbal remedies contain active plant chemicals that can cause dangerous drug interactions or affect pregnancy. [learn more](BMP124_U1_T3#BMP124_U1_T3_h7)

question: A pregnant woman in labor admits to drinking a local herbal mixture to speed up contractions. What is the most appropriate action for the midwife?

options.A: Assume the herbal drink is completely inert water with no physiological effect
options.B: Immediately discharge the patient home without further monitoring
options.C: Assess uterine activity closely and document the herbal intake in her clinical record
options.D: Scold the patient severely for ignoring orthodox medical advice

explanation: Documenting and monitoring is important because plant-based oxytocic compounds can cause uterine hyperstimulation. [learn more](BMP124_U1_T3#BMP124_U1_T3_h7)

question: What does the term pharmacokinetics primarily describe?

options.A: How diseases spread in a community
options.B: What a drug does to the body
options.C: What the body does to a drug
options.D: How herbs interact with modern drugs

explanation: Pharmacokinetics focuses on how the body handles a medication through absorption, distribution, metabolism, and excretion. [learn more](BMP124_U1_T4#BMP124_U1_T4_h1)

question: Which set of letters correctly represents the four main stages of pharmacokinetics?

options.A: ASTH
options.B: APNC
options.C: ADME
options.D: ABCD

explanation: The stages stand for Absorption, Distribution, Metabolism, and Excretion. [learn more](BMP124_U1_T4#BMP124_U1_T4_h1)

question: Which administration route completely bypasses the absorption phase?

options.A: Sublingual spray
options.B: Intramuscular injection
options.C: Oral tablet
options.D: Intravenous injection

explanation: Giving a drug straight into a vein puts it directly into the circulation, meaning no absorption step is needed. [learn more](BMP124_U1_T4#BMP124_U1_T4_h2)

question: Why is oral drug absorption often delayed during pregnancy?

options.A: Gastric acid production drops to zero
options.B: Liver enzymes stop working completely
options.C: Gastrointestinal motility slows down
options.D: Blood flow to the stomach increases

explanation: High progesterone levels during pregnancy relax smooth muscle, slowing down gut movement and delaying how fast drugs enter the blood. [learn more](BMP124_U1_T4#BMP124_U1_T4_h2)

question: What type of drug molecule can cross biological membranes and have an effect?

options.A: Unbound free drugs
options.B: Protein-bound drugs
options.C: Heavy metal complexes
options.D: Large fat globules

explanation: Only drugs that are not attached to plasma proteins are small and active enough to slip across membranes to target sites. [learn more](BMP124_U1_T4#BMP124_U1_T4_h3)

question: A pregnant patient receives a water-soluble antibiotic. How might the large increase in her body water affect the drug?

options.A: It will stay entirely in her fat tissues
options.B: It may require higher doses to reach effective levels
options.C: It will turn into a solid crystal in the blood
options.D: It will fail to cross the placenta completely

explanation: More body fluid dilutes water-soluble medicines, meaning standard doses might be too weak to work effectively. [learn more](BMP124_U1_T4#BMP124_U1_T4_h3)

question: Which organ is primarily responsible for metabolizing most drugs in the body?

options.A: Kidney
options.B: Spleen
options.C: Pancreas
options.D: Liver

explanation: The liver contains specialized enzyme systems that break down and alter drug molecules. [learn more](BMP124_U1_T4#BMP124_U1_T4_h4)

question: What is the main purpose of drug metabolism?

options.A: To increase blood pressure rapidly
options.B: To turn drugs into water-soluble forms for easy removal
options.C: To make every drug stick permanently to fat tissues
options.D: To stop the stomach from absorbing food

explanation: Metabolism changes fat-loving drug molecules into water-friendly waste products that the kidneys can filter out. [learn more](BMP124_U1_T4#BMP124_U1_T4_h4)

question: Which organ serves as the primary site for drug excretion?

options.A: Lungs
options.B: Kidneys
options.C: Skin
options.D: Heart

explanation: The kidneys filter blood and pass water-soluble drug waste out through the urine. [learn more](BMP124_U1_T4#BMP124_U1_T4_h5)

question: How does normal pregnancy affect the clearance of drugs that leave the body through the kidneys?

options.A: Clearance stays exactly the same as in non-pregnant women
options.B: Clearance is faster because kidney filtration increases
options.C: Clearance stops completely until after childbirth
options.D: Clearance is slower due to blocked ureters

explanation: Pregnant women have a higher glomerular filtration rate, meaning kidney-cleared drugs leave the system quicker. [learn more](BMP124_U1_T4#BMP124_U1_T4_h5)

question: A midwife notes that a pregnant patient needs an increased dose of a renally cleared drug to maintain therapeutic levels. What physiological change best explains this?

options.A: Decreased overall body weight
options.B: Total shutdown of liver enzymes
options.C: Increased glomerular filtration rate
options.D: Higher levels of stomach acid

explanation: Faster kidney filtration pushes the drug out of the blood quicker, often necessitating higher or more frequent doses. [learn more](BMP124_U1_T4#BMP124_U1_T4_h6)

question: Which of the following is NOT a typical pharmacokinetic change seen during pregnancy?

options.A: Altered liver enzyme activity
options.B: Increased renal clearance
options.C: Decreased total body water volume
options.D: Elevated plasma volume

explanation: Total body water actually increases substantially during pregnancy, rather than decreasing. [learn more](BMP124_U1_T4#BMP124_U1_T4_h6)

question: What is the primary focus of pharmacodynamics?

options.A: What a drug does to the body
options.B: How the liver breaks down active drugs
options.C: The rate at which a drug is excreted
options.D: How the body absorbs a medication

explanation: Pharmacodynamics looks at the biological and physiological effects that drugs produce inside the body. [learn more](BMP124_U1_T5#BMP124_U1_T5_h1)

question: Why is it important for a midwife to understand pharmacodynamics?

options.A: To trace the metabolic pathway of drugs through the liver
options.B: To understand how drugs trigger therapeutic and side effects
options.C: To calculate the exact speed of drug excretion by the kidneys
options.D: To determine how quickly oral tablets dissolve in the stomach

explanation: Knowing how drugs work helps midwives anticipate clinical responses and manage potential complications safely. [learn more](BMP124_U1_T5#BMP124_U1_T5_h1)

question: Which term describes how strongly a drug is attracted to its target receptor?

options.A: Metabolism
options.B: Affinity
options.C: Potency
options.D: Tolerance

explanation: Affinity refers to how strongly a drug is attracted to and binds with its specific cellular receptor. [learn more](BMP124_U1_T5#BMP124_U1_T5_h2)

question: What happens right after a drug molecule successfully binds to its target receptor?

options.A: The liver metabolizes the compound into an inactive state
options.B: A cascade of biochemical changes is initiated inside the cell
options.C: The drug is immediately excreted by the renal system
options.D: The receptor is permanently destroyed to prevent overuse

explanation: Drug-receptor binding acts like a key in a lock, triggering internal cellular changes that result in a physiological effect. [learn more](BMP124_U1_T5#BMP124_U1_T5_h2)

question: Which type of drug binds to a receptor and blocks natural chemicals from activating it?

options.A: Catalyst
options.B: Agonist
options.C: Antagonist
options.D: Enzyme

explanation: Antagonists attach to receptors without activating them, blocking other substances from producing an effect. [learn more](BMP124_U1_T5#BMP124_U1_T5_h3)

question: A newborn shows signs of slow breathing due to labor pain relief medication. Which drug category is used to reverse this?

options.A: Full agonist
options.B: Antagonist
options.C: Enzyme inhibitor
options.D: Partial agonist

explanation: An opioid antagonist like naloxone is used to block opioid receptors and reverse respiratory depression in the neonate. [learn more](BMP124_U1_T5#BMP124_U1_T5_h3)

question: What does the term 'potency' mean in pharmacology?

options.A: The speed at which a drug is cleared from blood
options.B: The tendency of a drug to cause adverse reactions
options.C: The maximum possible effect a drug can produce
options.D: The amount of drug needed to produce a specific effect

explanation: Potency measures the dose concentration required to achieve a desired biological response. [learn more](BMP124_U1_T5#BMP124_U1_T5_h4)

question: Why does increasing a drug's dose eventually stop producing a stronger effect?

options.A: The drug transforms into an inactive antagonist
options.B: The liver destroys the extra medication instantly
options.C: All available cellular receptors are fully occupied
options.D: The kidneys begin excreting the drug too quickly

explanation: Once every receptor is bound by the drug, reaching the ceiling effect, adding more medication cannot increase the response. [learn more](BMP124_U1_T5#BMP124_U1_T5_h4)

question: What does a narrow therapeutic index mean for a medication?

options.A: It is completely safe to administer without monitoring
options.B: It is broken down too quickly by the digestive system
options.C: It requires very large doses to achieve any clinical effect
options.D: There is a small margin of safety between efficacy and toxicity

explanation: A narrow therapeutic index means the dose required for treatment is very close to the dose that causes toxicity. [learn more](BMP124_U1_T5#BMP124_U1_T5_h5)

question: Which of the following statements is NOT true about drugs with a narrow therapeutic index?

options.A: The difference between healing and harm is very small
options.B: They require careful clinical monitoring of the patient
options.C: They can be administered in excessive doses safely
options.D: Toxic blood levels may lead to life-threatening complications

explanation: Administering excessive doses of narrow therapeutic index drugs is extremely dangerous and can cause severe toxicity or death. [learn more](BMP124_U1_T5#BMP124_U1_T5_h5)

question: What do we call the study of how the body handles a drug after it is given?

options.A: Pharmacodynamics
options.B: Pharmacokinetics
options.C: Pharmacoepidemiology
options.D: Pharmacogenomics

explanation: Pharmacokinetics is the study of how a drug moves through the body, covering absorption, distribution, metabolism, and excretion. [learn more](BMP124_U1_T6#BMP124_U1_T6_h1)

question: Why might two pregnant women react completely differently to the exact same dose of a medicine?

options.A: The liver stops working completely during pregnancy
options.B: Standard hospital drug charts are always incorrect
options.C: Manufacturers intentionally vary tablet strengths in each batch
options.D: Biological variability affects how drugs are processed and received

explanation: Every person has different organ function, body composition, and genetics, which naturally changes how medications affect them. [learn more](BMP124_U1_T6#BMP124_U1_T6_h1)

question: Which organs are usually still developing in a newborn baby, making drug toxicity a higher risk?

options.A: Visual and auditory systems
options.B: Skeletal muscle system
options.C: Liver and kidneys
options.D: Upper respiratory tract

explanation: Babies have immature liver enzymes and lower kidney filtration, which slows down how fast their bodies clear out medications. [learn more](BMP124_U1_T6#BMP124_U1_T6_h2)

question: An elderly patient takes a standard adult dose of a water-soluble medicine. Which age-related change puts her at risk of toxicity?

options.A: Expanded plasma volume
options.B: Decreased total body water
options.C: Higher glomerular filtration rate
options.D: Increased liver enzyme production

explanation: Older adults have less total body water, which means water-soluble drugs concentrate in a smaller volume of fluid and reach higher levels in the blood. [learn more](BMP124_U1_T6#BMP124_U1_T6_h2)

question: Where do fat-soluble drugs mainly store themselves in a patient with a high body fat percentage?

options.A: Bone marrow matrix
options.B: Red blood cells
options.C: Gastric mucosa
options.D: Adipose tissue

explanation: Fat-soluble drugs settle easily into fatty or adipose tissues, which can trap the drug and keep it active in the body for a longer time. [learn more](BMP124_U1_T6#BMP124_U1_T6_h3)

question: Why can giving a standard adult drug dose be dangerous for a severely malnourished patient?

options.A: Body fat increases rapidly during starvation
options.B: Altered protein binding can lead to higher levels of active free drug
options.C: The digestive tract destroys all medications instantly
options.D: Malnourished patients have faster kidney clearance rates

explanation: Low blood protein means fewer binding sites for the medicine, leaving more free drug circulating in the blood and raising the risk of side effects. [learn more](BMP124_U1_T6#BMP124_U1_T6_h3)

question: What are patients called who break down medications much slower than usual due to their genes?

options.A: Ultra-rapid metabolizers
options.B: Poor metabolizers
options.C: Resistant absorbers
options.D: Hyper-excretors

explanation: Poor metabolizers have inherited traits that lower their enzyme activity, meaning drugs stay active in their systems much longer. [learn more](BMP124_U1_T6#BMP124_U1_T6_h4)

question: What usually happens when an ultra-rapid metabolizer takes a standard dose of a medicine?

options.A: Severe toxicity from immediate drug accumulation
options.B: Therapeutic failure because the drug is cleared too quickly
options.C: Total blockage of gastrointestinal absorption
options.D: Permanent deactivation of liver enzymes

explanation: If enzymes process a medicine too fast, blood levels drop before the drug has a chance to help the patient. [learn more](BMP124_U1_T6#BMP124_U1_T6_h4)

question: Which health issue makes it hardest for the body to get rid of water-soluble drugs?

options.A: Renal impairment
options.B: Myocardial ischemia
options.C: Gastric hyperacidity
options.D: Pulmonary congestion

explanation: The kidneys filter out water-soluble drugs, so when kidney function is low, these medications build up in the bloodstream. [learn more](BMP124_U1_T6#BMP124_U1_T6_h5)

question: A patient with severe liver disease is given a standard dose of a drug that the liver normally breaks down. What is the likely result?

options.A: Rapid elimination of the drug through the skin
options.B: Increased risk of drug toxicity due to reduced metabolism

question: What happens when one medicine changes how the body handles a second medicine taken at the same time?

options.A: A genetic polymorphism

options.D: Physiological tolerance

explanation: A drug-drug interaction occurs when two or more substances mix in the body and alter each other's effects or safety. [learn more](BMP124_U1_T6#BMP124_U1_T6_h6)

question: Why should midwives always ask pregnant women about local herbal remedies during antenatal visits?

options.A: Herbs contain active chemical compounds that can interact with prescribed drugs
options.B: Traditional mixtures replace the need for routine iron supplementation
options.C: Herbal preparations always double the rate of fetal growth
options.D: Local herbs completely neutralize all hospital medications

explanation: Herbal remedies act like medicines in the body and can interfere with prescribed treatments or cause unexpected side effects. [learn more](BMP124_U1_T6#BMP124_U1_T6_h6)

question: What body functions are primarily controlled by the autonomic nervous system?

options.A: Involuntary functions like heart rate
options.B: Skeletal muscle coordination for walking
options.C: Conscious thought and memory recall
options.D: Voluntary muscle movement of limbs

explanation: The autonomic nervous system handles automatic body processes that do not require conscious control, such as heart rate and digestion. [learn more](BMP124_U2_T1#BMP124_U2_T1_h1)

question: Why is it important for a midwife to understand autonomic pharmacology?

options.A: To replace the need for physical pelvic examinations
options.B: To diagnose complex brain disorders during pregnancy
options.C: To calculate exact doses of routine daily vitamins
options.D: To safely manage blood pressure and uterine activity

explanation: Autonomic drugs directly influence the uterus and cardiovascular system, making this knowledge vital for obstetric safety. [learn more](BMP124_U2_T1#BMP124_U2_T1_h1)

question: Which division of the autonomic nervous system drives the fight-or-flight response?

options.A: Central spinal nerve system
options.B: Parasympathetic nervous system
options.C: Sympathetic nervous system
options.D: Somatic motor nervous system

explanation: The sympathetic system prepares the body to react quickly during stressful or emergency situations. [learn more](BMP124_U2_T1#BMP124_U2_T1_h2)

question: What is the primary role of the parasympathetic nervous system?

options.A: Releasing hormones for immediate muscle contraction
options.B: Increasing heart rate during sudden physical threats
options.C: Directing voluntary movement of the arms and legs
options.D: Conserving energy and handling rest-and-digest tasks

explanation: Parasympathetic pathways focus on maintenance activities like digestion and slowing down the heart rate during calm periods. [learn more](BMP124_U2_T1#BMP124_U2_T1_h2)

question: Which two main neurotransmitters are primarily used in the autonomic nervous system?

options.A: Serotonin and dopamine
options.B: Acetylcholine and norepinephrine
options.C: Histamine and cortisol
options.D: Insulin and glucagon

explanation: These two chemicals are the principal messengers responsible for transmitting signals across autonomic nerve pathways. [learn more](BMP124_U2_T1#BMP124_U2_T1_h3)

question: What type of receptors respond to norepinephrine?

options.A: Nicotinic receptors
options.B: Adrenergic receptors
options.C: Muscarinic receptors
options.D: Cholinergic receptors

explanation: Adrenergic receptors are specifically activated by norepinephrine and epinephrine in the sympathetic nervous system. [learn more](BMP124_U2_T1#BMP124_U2_T1_h3)

question: What effect does a sympathomimetic drug typically have on the body?

options.A: It promotes active digestion and salivation
options.B: It slows down breathing and heart rate
options.C: It lowers blood pressure by relaxing vessels
options.D: It mimics the fight-or-flight response

explanation: Sympathomimetic drugs stimulate sympathetic pathways, producing effects similar to natural adrenaline. [learn more](BMP124_U2_T1#BMP124_U2_T1_h4)

question: Which of the following is NOT a typical effect of an anticholinergic drug?

options.A: Dry mouth and reduced secretions
options.B: A faster resting heart rate
options.C: Relaxation of certain smooth muscles
options.D: Increased saliva and digestive juices

explanation: Anticholinergic drugs block parasympathetic action, which actually dries up secretions rather than increasing them. [learn more](BMP124_U2_T1#BMP124_U2_T1_h4)

question: How does a receptor agonist work?

options.A: It blocks a receptor to stop action
options.B: It binds to a receptor and activates it
options.C: It prevents the release of hormones
options.D: It destroys excess neurotransmitters

explanation: Agonists successfully trigger the receptor to produce a cellular response similar to the body's own chemicals. [learn more](BMP124_U2_T1#BMP124_U2_T1_h5)

question: What happens when a drug acts as a receptor antagonist?

options.A: It transforms the target receptor into a different type of protein
options.B: It occupies the receptor without turning it on, blocking other signals
options.C: It forces the receptor to produce double the normal chemical output
options.D: It permanently destroys the nerve cell membrane to stop pain

explanation: Antagonists sit on the receptor like a decoy, preventing the natural neurotransmitter from attaching and creating an effect. [learn more](BMP124_U2_T1#BMP124_U2_T1_h5)

question: Why might a clinician administer a beta-agonist drug to a pregnant woman?

options.A: To raise the baby's heart rate during fetal distress
options.B: To speed up cervical dilation during active pushing
options.C: To induce heavy bleeding after placental delivery
options.D: To relax the uterine muscle and delay preterm labour

explanation: Beta-agonists relax smooth muscle in the uterus, making them useful for temporarily stopping premature contractions. [learn more](BMP124_U2_T1#BMP124_U2_T1_h6)

question: How do medications managing severe pre-eclampsia relate to the autonomic system?

options.A: They block all neurological impulses to eliminate labour pain completely
options.B: They stimulate parasympathetic nerves to increase the mother's appetite
options.C: They replace natural hormones required for fetal lung development
options.D: They often target autonomic receptors to lower dangerously high blood pressure

explanation: Drugs managing pre-eclampsia frequently act on blood vessels via autonomic pathways to prevent maternal stroke or organ damage. [learn more](BMP124_U2_T1#BMP124_U2_T1_h6)

question: Why do autonomic drugs frequently cause side effects in other parts of the body?

options.A: They only work when the patient is under severe stress
options.B: The drugs dissolve too quickly inside the digestive tract
options.C: They change the chemical composition of the mother's blood
options.D: The same type of receptors are found in multiple different organs

explanation: Because receptors like adrenergic and cholinergic types exist across the heart, lungs, and blood vessels, a drug cannot easily target just one organ. [learn more](BMP124_U2_T1#BMP124_U2_T1_h7)

question: What common maternal side effect is often seen when using beta-agonists to stop contractions?

options.A: Complete loss of vision
options.B: Paralysis of the legs
options.C: Rapid heart rate
options.D: Severe drop in temperature

explanation: Beta-agonists stimulate heart receptors as well as uterine receptors, frequently leading to maternal tachycardia. [learn more](BMP124_U2_T1#BMP124_U2_T1_h7)

question: What part of the nervous system do sympathomimetic drugs mimic?

options.A: Enteric nervous system
options.B: Somatic nervous system
options.C: Sympathetic nervous system
options.D: Parasympathetic nervous system

explanation: Sympathomimetic drugs copy the actions of the sympathetic nervous system, which triggers fight-or-flight responses. [learn more](BMP124_U2_T2#BMP124_U2_T2_h1)

question: Which natural chemical is a primary messenger for the adrenergic system?

options.A: Epinephrine
options.B: Dopamine
options.C: Serotonin
options.D: Acetylcholine

explanation: Epinephrine and norepinephrine are the primary natural catecholamines that activate the adrenergic system in the body. [learn more](BMP124_U2_T2#BMP124_U2_T2_h1)

question: Where are Beta-1 receptors mainly located in the body?

options.A: Kidneys
options.B: Heart
options.C: Skin
options.D: Lungs

explanation: Beta-1 receptors are mostly found in the heart, where their stimulation increases heart rate and the strength of contractions. [learn more](BMP124_U2_T2#BMP124_U2_T2_h2)

question: Which receptor type causes the uterine muscle to relax when stimulated?

options.A: Beta-2 receptors
options.B: Beta-1 receptors
options.C: Alpha-1 receptors
options.D: Alpha-2 receptors

explanation: Stimulation of Beta-2 receptors causes smooth muscles to relax, including the myometrium of the uterus and airways in the lungs. [learn more](BMP124_U2_T2#BMP124_U2_T2_h2)

question: Why might a clinician give a beta-2 agonist during preterm contractions?

options.A: To speed up cervical dilation and delivery
options.B: To relax the uterine muscle and slow down labor
options.C: To increase blood clotting factors in the placenta
options.D: To stimulate milk production before birth

explanation: Beta-2 agonists relax smooth muscle, which helps slow down or temporarily stop uterine contractions during preterm labor. [learn more](BMP124_U2_T2#BMP124_U2_T2_h3)

question: A patient's blood pressure drops suddenly after spinal anesthesia for a caesarean section. Which drug type helps correct this?

options.A: Parasympathomimetic
options.B: Sedative hypnotic
options.C: Beta blocker
options.D: Vasopressor sympathomimetic

explanation: Vasopressors constrict blood vessels via alpha receptors, which quickly raises maternal blood pressure and restores blood flow to the placenta. [learn more](BMP124_U2_T2#BMP124_U2_T2_h3)

question: Which of these is NOT a typical side effect of a sympathomimetic drug?

options.A: Slow heart rate
options.B: Fine muscle tremors
options.C: High blood pressure
options.D: Rapid heart rate

explanation: Sympathomimetic drugs speed up body functions, so a slow heart rate is not expected. A fast heart rate is the normal finding. [learn more](BMP124_U2_T2#BMP124_U2_T2_h4)

question: Why do patients receiving adrenergic medications often feel anxious or shaky?

options.A: The drugs stimulate the central nervous system much like a stress response.
options.B: The drugs directly destroy red blood cells carrying oxygen to the brain.
options.C: The drugs cause a sudden drop in core body temperature.
options.D: The drugs block all electrical activity in peripheral nerves.

explanation: By mimicking fight-or-flight hormones, these medications naturally cause feelings of jitteriness, tremors, and anxiety. [learn more](BMP124_U2_T2#BMP124_U2_T2_h4)

question: Why is continuous foetal monitoring needed when a patient receives a potent sympathomimetic drug?

options.A: To check if the baby has a congenital heart defect
options.B: To measure the exact weight of the baby before birth
options.C: To detect any changes in uteroplacental blood flow caused by maternal blood pressure shifts
options.D: To determine the exact gestational age of the foetus

explanation: Maternal blood pressure changes can affect the blood supply reaching the placenta, making foetal monitoring essential to catch early signs of distress. [learn more](BMP124_U2_T2#BMP124_U2_T2_h5)

question: A midwife is preparing an intravenous sympathomimetic infusion in the labor ward. What safety measure comes first?

options.A: Diluting the medication in a large volume of sterile water only
options.B: Using an infusion pump and double-checking drug calculations
options.C: Administering the drug rapidly by hand to check the patient's reaction
options.D: Stopping all maternal fluid intake before starting the medication

explanation: Potent vasoactive drugs require electronic infusion control and double-checking to prevent dangerous rapid overdose or severe blood pressure spikes. [learn more](BMP124_U2_T2#BMP124_U2_T2_h5)

question: What is the main effect of sympatholytic drugs on the body?

options.A: They increase adrenaline in the blood
options.B: They slow down the sympathetic nervous system
options.C: They speed up the heart rate
options.D: They cause a fight-or-flight reaction

explanation: Sympatholytic drugs block the effects of the sympathetic nervous system, whereas sympathomimetic drugs stimulate it. [learn more](BMP124_U2_T3#BMP124_U2_T3_h1)

question: Why are adrenergic blocking drugs important in maternity care?

options.A: They help prevent bleeding after delivery
options.B: They help start contractions during labor
options.C: They help manage high blood pressure in pregnancy
options.D: They help the baby's lungs mature early

explanation: By blocking adrenergic receptors, these drugs lower blood pressure, which is essential for managing hypertensive disorders during pregnancy. [learn more](BMP124_U2_T3#BMP124_U2_T3_h1)

question: Where are alpha receptors mostly found in the body?

options.A: Smooth muscle of the uterus
options.B: Peripheral blood vessels
options.C: Air sacs of the lungs
options.D: The SA node of the heart

explanation: Alpha receptors are mainly located in peripheral blood vessels. When they are activated, blood vessels constrict, and when they are blocked, blood vessels dilate. [learn more](BMP124_U2_T3#BMP124_U2_T3_h2)

question: What is the main difference between beta-1 selective blockers and non-selective beta-blockers?

options.A: Beta-1 blockers target the heart, while non-selective blockers also affect the lungs
options.B: Beta-1 blockers are used only for pregnant women
options.C: Non-selective blockers only work on alpha receptors
options.D: Beta-1 blockers raise blood pressure while non-selective ones lower it

explanation: Beta-1 receptors are mostly found in the heart, so selective blockers act there. Non-selective blockers also affect beta-2 receptors in areas like the lungs. [learn more](BMP124_U2_T3#BMP124_U2_T3_h2)

question: How do sympatholytic drugs interact with adrenergic receptors?

options.A: They turn beta receptors into alpha receptors
options.B: They destroy the receptor proteins completely
options.C: They occupy receptor sites without activating them
options.D: They destroy adrenaline molecules in the blood

explanation: They act as blockers by attaching to the receptors so natural hormones cannot bind, which prevents the usual cellular response. [learn more](BMP124_U2_T3#BMP124_U2_T3_h3)

question: What happens when a beta-blocker attaches to beta-1 receptors on the heart?

options.A: Calcium floods into the heart cells quickly
options.B: The heart contracts much more strongly
options.C: Heart rate and oxygen demand decrease
options.D: Coronary arteries go into severe spasm

explanation: Blocking beta-1 receptors reduces the workload of the heart, lowering both the heart rate and how hard it works. [learn more](BMP124_U2_T3#BMP124_U2_T3_h3)

question: Which of the following is a direct effect of beta-blockers on the heart?

options.A: Narrowing of coronary vessels
options.B: Decreased heart rate
options.C: Faster electrical signals in the heart
options.D: Increased pumping output

explanation: Beta-blockers slow down the heart rate by reducing the speed of electrical signals in the heart's conduction system. [learn more](BMP124_U2_T3#BMP124_U2_T3_h4)

question: What is a potential risk when using non-selective beta-blockers in patients with breathing problems?

options.A: Rapid expansion of lung capacity
options.B: Relaxation of the airways
options.C: Increased oxygen exchange
options.D: Tightening of the airways

explanation: Non-selective beta-blockers can block beta-2 receptors in the lungs and cause the airways to narrow, which is dangerous for patients with asthma. [learn more](BMP124_U2_T3#BMP124_U2_T3_h4)

question: What is the main reason midwives use sympatholytic drugs like labetalol?

options.A: To help start labor contractions
options.B: To prevent early miscarriage
options.C: To manage high blood pressure in pregnancy
options.D: To manage post-term pregnancies

explanation: Midwives and doctors use these medications to control high blood pressure conditions such as preeclampsia during pregnancy. [learn more](BMP124_U2_T3#BMP124_U2_T3_h5)

question: A pregnant woman at 34 weeks has a blood pressure reading of 160/110 mmHg. Which drug class is most appropriate to start?

options.A: Uterotonic oxytocic agents
options.B: Sympathomimetic stimulants
options.C: Sympatholytic antihypertensives
options.D: Beta-adrenergic agonists

explanation: Severe high blood pressure in pregnancy requires blood pressure-lowering drugs like sympatholytics to protect the mother from complications. [learn more](BMP124_U2_T3#BMP124_U2_T3_h5)

question: Which of the following is a common side effect of sympatholytic therapy?

options.A: Inability to sleep
options.B: Slow heart rate
options.C: Fast heart rate
options.D: High blood pressure

explanation: Because these medications slow down the heart, a slow heart rate (bradycardia) is a common side effect that requires regular monitoring. [learn more](BMP124_U2_T3#BMP124_U2_T3_h6)

question: Why is monitoring the baby important when a pregnant patient receives intravenous labetalol for high blood pressure?

options.A: Sudden drops in maternal blood pressure can reduce blood flow to the placenta
options.B: The baby will completely stop moving while the drug is active
options.C: The baby's blood sugar drops during the infusion
options.D: The drug crosses the placenta to speed up the baby's heart

explanation: If maternal blood pressure drops too quickly, blood flow to the placenta decreases, which can cause distress for the baby. [learn more](BMP124_U2_T3#BMP124_U2_T3_h6)

question: Which vital sign check is most important before giving a beta-blocker?

options.A: Respiratory rate
options.B: Body temperature
options.C: Pulse rate
options.D: Blood glucose level

explanation: The pulse rate must be checked before giving a beta-blocker to ensure the patient's heart rate is not already too low. [learn more](BMP124_U2_T3#BMP124_U2_T3_h7)

question: A postpartum mother taking an alpha-blocker feels dizzy when she stands up quickly. What is the best advice to give her?

options.A: Rise slowly from a sitting or lying position
options.B: Exercise vigorously to boost circulation
options.C: Stop taking the prescribed medication immediately
options.D: Drink extra cups of coffee

explanation: Dizziness upon standing is caused by blood pressure dropping when blood vessels dilate. Changing positions gradually helps prevent this. [learn more](BMP124_U2_T3#BMP124_U2_T3_h7)

question: What is another common name for parasympathomimetic drugs?

options.A: Adrenergic drugs
options.B: Cholinergic drugs
options.C: Anticholinergic drugs
options.D: Sympathomimetic drugs

explanation: Parasympathomimetic drugs mimic the parasympathetic nervous system and are widely known as cholinergic drugs because they work with acetylcholine. [learn more](BMP124_U2_T4#BMP124_U2_T4_h1)

question: Which body state is primarily promoted by the parasympathetic nervous system?

options.A: Stress and panic
options.B: High adrenaline
options.C: Fight or flight
options.D: Rest and digest

explanation: The parasympathetic system handles resting, digesting, and conserving energy, unlike the sympathetic system which prepares the body for high stress. [learn more](BMP124_U2_T4#BMP124_U2_T4_h1)

question: Where are muscarinic receptors primarily located in the body?

options.A: Smooth muscle, cardiac muscle, and glands
options.B: Only within the central brain cortex
options.C: The outer layer of the skin and hair follicles
options.D: Skeletal muscle and bone marrow only

explanation: Muscarinic receptors sit on target organs of the parasympathetic nervous system, including smooth muscles, the heart, and various glands. [learn more](BMP124_U2_T4#BMP124_U2_T4_h2)

question: How do indirect cholinergic agonists increase activity at the receptor?

options.A: By speeding up the creation of new nerve cells
options.B: By destroying extra receptors on the target tissue
options.C: By replacing acetylcholine with synthetic hormones
options.D: By blocking the enzyme that destroys acetylcholine

explanation: Indirect agents stop acetylcholinesterase from breaking down acetylcholine, which lets it build up and stimulate receptors longer. [learn more](BMP124_U2_T4#BMP124_U2_T4_h2)

question: Which medication is an example of a direct-acting cholinergic agonist?

options.A: Neostigmine
options.B: Atropine
options.C: Adrenaline
options.D: Bethanechol

explanation: Bethanechol binds straight to the cholinergic receptors to stimulate the bladder, making it a direct-acting agent. [learn more](BMP124_U2_T4#BMP124_U2_T4_h3)

question: What is the primary difference in how direct and indirect agonists work?

options.A: Direct agents lower blood pressure, while indirect agents always raise blood pressure
options.B: Direct agents only work in the brain, while indirect agents work only in the gut
options.C: Direct agents bind to receptors themselves, while indirect agents prevent acetylcholine breakdown
options.D: Direct agents are natural herbs, while indirect agents are strictly lab-made chemicals

explanation: Direct agonists act as fake keys for the lock, whereas indirect agonists keep the body's natural keys from being thrown away. [learn more](BMP124_U2_T4#BMP124_U2_T4_h3)

question: What effect do cholinergic drugs typically have on the pupils of the eyes?

options.A: Complete paralysis
options.B: Constriction (miosis)
options.C: Rapid blinking
options.D: Dilating very wide

explanation: Parasympathetic stimulation causes the circular muscles of the iris to contract, leading to pupil constriction known as miosis. [learn more](BMP124_U2_T4#BMP124_U2_T4_h4)

question: A patient is given a strong cholinergic medication. Which finding is most likely to be observed during assessment?

options.A: Inability to urinate due to bladder relaxation
options.B: A very fast resting heart rate and high fever
options.C: Dry mouth, constipation, and dilated pupils
options.D: Increased watery saliva and abdominal cramping

explanation: Cholinergic drugs stimulate secretions and smooth muscle activity, leading to lots of saliva and active bowel movements or cramps. [learn more](BMP124_U2_T4#BMP124_U2_T4_h4)

question: What is a primary clinical use of cholinergic drugs like bethanechol in postpartum care?

options.A: Treating urinary retention
options.B: Speeding up cervical dilation
options.C: Stopping severe postpartum bleeding
options.D: Lowering high blood pressure

question: Why might a midwife encounter a cholinergic-related drug following a surgical procedure in obstetrics?

options.A: To dry up breast milk secretions after delivery
options.B: To induce immediate labor contractions in a preterm client
options.C: To prevent the development of gestational diabetes
options.D: To reverse muscle relaxants used during anesthesia

explanation: Indirect cholinergic agents are frequently administered alongside anticholinergic drugs to reverse neuromuscular blockade after surgery. [learn more](BMP124_U2_T4#BMP124_U2_T4_h5)

question: Which drug is the standard emergency antidote for severe cholinergic toxicity?

options.A: Atropine
options.B: Bethanechol
options.C: Magnesium sulfate
options.D: Adrenaline

explanation: Atropine blocks muscarinic receptors and quickly reverses the life-threatening secretions and bronchospasm of a cholinergic crisis. [learn more](BMP124_U2_T4#BMP124_U2_T4_h6)

question: Which of the following is NOT a classic symptom of cholinergic toxicity?

options.A: Cramping diarrhea and frequent urination
options.B: Extreme dryness of the skin and mouth
options.C: Excessive tearing and watery eyes
options.D: Profuse sweating and heavy salivation

explanation: Cholinergic toxicity causes wet symptoms like sweating, tearing, and salivation, whereas dry skin and mouth point to anticholinergic effects. [learn more](BMP124_U2_T4#BMP124_U2_T4_h6)

question: Why are cholinergic drugs strictly contraindicated in clients with a physical intestinal blockage?

options.A: The patient will experience severe hair loss and skin rashes
options.B: The medication will instantly dissolve and cause systemic poisoning
options.C: Increased muscle contractions can cause the blocked organ to rupture
options.D: Blocked intestines completely destroy the active molecules of the drug

explanation: Forcing a blocked bowel or bladder to contract harder with a cholinergic drug creates dangerous pressure that can lead to perforation. [learn more](BMP124_U2_T4#BMP124_U2_T4_h7)

question: A midwife is caring for a client with a history of severe asthma who is prescribed a cholinergic drug. What is the main risk?

options.A: Triggering a dangerous asthma attack through bronchospasm
options.B: Causing a sudden and permanent rise in blood pressure
options.C: Causing severe insomnia and nervous system excitement
options.D: Stopping the kidneys from producing any urine at all

explanation: Cholinergic stimulation constricts the airways, which can easily trigger a severe bronchospasm in someone with asthma. [learn more](BMP124_U2_T4#BMP124_U2_T4_h7)

question: What is another common name for parasympatholytic drugs?

options.A: Cholinergic agonists
options.B: Sympathomimetics
options.C: Anticholinergics
options.D: Beta-blockers

explanation: Parasympatholytics block acetylcholine and are widely known as anticholinergic agents because they oppose the effects of the parasympathetic nervous system. [learn more](BMP124_U2_T5#BMP124_U2_T5_h1)

question: Why are parasympatholytics described as shifting the body toward sympathetic dominance?

options.A: They release adrenaline directly
options.B: They block rest and digest activity
options.C: They stimulate alpha receptors in vessels
options.D: They increase heart rate via the spinal cord

explanation: By shutting down the resting parasympathetic tone, the body naturally exhibits signs of sympathetic dominance like increased heart rate and dry secretions. [learn more](BMP124_U2_T5#BMP124_U2_T5_h1)

question: Which specific receptor type do classical parasympatholytics block?

options.A: Adrenergic receptors
options.B: Nicotinic receptors
options.C: Muscarinic receptors
options.D: Dopaminergic receptors

explanation: Classical parasympatholytics specifically target and block muscarinic acetylcholine receptors located on peripheral effector organs. [learn more](BMP124_U2_T5#BMP124_U2_T5_h2)

question: What happens when an anticholinergic drug binds to a muscarinic receptor?

options.A: It opens the channel for massive calcium influx
options.B: It mimics acetylcholine to speed up organ function
options.C: It permanently destroys the receptor protein
options.D: It blocks the receptor without activating it

explanation: Competitive antagonists occupy the binding site so acetylcholine cannot attach, but they do not trigger the cellular response themselves. [learn more](BMP124_U2_T5#BMP124_U2_T5_h2)

question: Which eye effect is caused by anticholinergic drugs?

options.A: Uncontrolled blinking
options.B: Excessive tearing
options.C: Pupil dilation
options.D: Pupil constriction

explanation: Anticholinergics relax the circular muscle of the iris, leading to mydriasis or pupil dilation. [learn more](BMP124_U2_T5#BMP124_U2_T5_h3)

question: A patient receiving an anticholinergic medication has difficulty passing urine. Which action caused this?

options.A: Complete failure of the kidneys to produce urine
options.B: Sudden enlargement of the prostate gland
options.C: Relaxation of the bladder detrusor muscle
options.D: Strong contraction of the urethral sphincter

explanation: Anticholinergics relax the bladder muscle, making it hard for the patient to void, which results in urinary retention. [learn more](BMP124_U2_T5#BMP124_U2_T5_h3)

question: What is a main reason for giving intravenous atropine in an emergency?

options.A: Extreme hypertension
options.B: Acute postpartum hemorrhage
options.C: Severe bradycardia
options.D: Sudden anaphylactic shock

explanation: Atropine blocks vagal input to the heart, safely increasing a dangerously low heart rate during emergencies. [learn more](BMP124_U2_T5#BMP124_U2_T5_h4)

question: Why is atropine sometimes given before surgery and anesthesia?

options.A: To relax all the skeletal muscles fully
options.B: To put the patient into a deep sleep
options.C: To prevent sudden postpartum bleeding
options.D: To reduce respiratory and oral secretions

explanation: Drying up airway and salivary secretions prevents the patient from choking or aspirating mucus while under anesthesia. [learn more](BMP124_U2_T5#BMP124_U2_T5_h4)

question: How does the skin typically look in severe anticholinergic toxicity?

options.A: Yellow as a lemon
options.B: Blue as a plum
options.C: Red as a beet
options.D: Pale as a ghost

explanation: Cutaneous blood vessels dilate to help shed heat when sweating fails, giving the skin a flushed, red appearance. [learn more](BMP124_U2_T5#BMP124_U2_T5_h5)

question: Why does an overdose of an anticholinergic drug cause a high body temperature?

options.A: The drug prevents sweating
options.B: It speeds up cellular metabolism
options.C: It causes severe muscle shivering

question: Why must anticholinergic drugs be avoided in a patient with angle-closure glaucoma?

question: What is the main effect of giving opioids to a woman in labour?

options.A: It destroys the local blood supply to the painful area
options.B: It forces the heart to pump blood at a much faster rate
options.C: It stops electrical nerve impulses from traveling to the brain
options.D: It immediately cools down the skin tissue around the wound

explanation: Without sodium movement, nerve fibers cannot carry pain messages upward to the central nervous system. [learn more](BMP124_U3_T5#BMP124_U3_T5_h4)

question: How do anaesthetic drugs primarily cross over from the mother to the fetus?

options.A: Direct injection into the umbilical cord
options.B: Simple diffusion across the placenta
options.C: Active transport via fetal red blood cells
options.D: Swallowing through the amniotic fluid

explanation: Most small molecular drugs easily cross the placental barrier and enter the fetal circulation. [learn more](BMP124_U3_T5#BMP124_U3_T5_h5)

question: What is a primary reason to monitor maternal blood pressure closely after an epidural block?

options.A: To confirm that the kidneys have stopped producing urine
options.B: To verify that the baby is breathing independently inside the womb
options.C: To ensure the mother's blood pressure rises above normal limits
options.D: To catch sudden drops that can reduce blood flow to the baby

explanation: Epidurals can cause maternal blood pressure to fall, which decreases the oxygen supply reaching the fetus through the placenta. [learn more](BMP124_U3_T5#BMP124_U3_T5_h5)

question: Which of the following is NOT an early warning sign of local anaesthetic systemic toxicity?

options.A: A sudden spike in scalp hair growth
options.B: Ringing sounds inside the ears
options.C: Numbness around the lips and mouth
options.D: A strange metallic taste in the mouth

explanation: Hair growth is completely unrelated to anaesthetic toxicity, whereas mouth numbness, metallic taste, and ringing ears are classic early warnings. [learn more](BMP124_U3_T5#BMP124_U3_T5_h6)

question: A woman receiving an epidural suddenly complains of a metallic taste and ringing in her ears. What immediate action should be taken?

options.A: Reassure her that this is a normal, harmless side effect of labor
options.B: Increase the speed of the anaesthetic drug delivery immediately
options.C: Stop the infusion and prepare for potential toxicity management
options.D: Encourage her to drink plenty of cold water to clear her palate

explanation: A metallic taste and ear ringing are classic early signs of local anaesthetic entering the bloodstream, requiring an immediate halt to the medication. [learn more](BMP124_U3_T5#BMP124_U3_T5_h6)

question: What is the main job of an anticonvulsant during pregnancy?

options.A: Preventing gestational diabetes
options.B: Stopping acute seizures like eclampsia
options.C: Lowering long-term blood pressure
options.D: Starting active labor contractions

explanation: Anticonvulsants are used to stop or prevent dangerous seizure episodes, such as eclampsia, in pregnant women. [learn more](BMP124_U3_T6#BMP124_U3_T6_h1)

question: How do routine antiepileptic drugs differ from emergency anticonvulsants?

options.A: Antiepileptics are only given through a drip during labor
options.B: Antiepileptics are herbal remedies with no side effects
options.C: Antiepileptics are used exclusively to speed up labor
options.D: Antiepileptics provide long-term daily control for chronic seizures

explanation: Chronic epilepsy requires ongoing daily medication to prevent seizures from happening over time. [learn more](BMP124_U3_T6#BMP124_U3_T6_h1)

question: Which medication is the first choice for treating eclamptic fits?

options.A: Hydralazine
options.B: Magnesium sulphate
options.C: Diazepam
options.D: Phenytoin

explanation: Magnesium sulphate is the standard, safest drug used to stop and prevent eclamptic fits. [learn more](BMP124_U3_T6#BMP124_U3_T6_h2)

question: A woman receiving a magnesium sulphate infusion has no knee-jerk reflexes. What should the midwife do first?

options.A: Give a dose of oral blood pressure medicine
options.B: Speed up the infusion to bring the reflex back
options.C: Encourage the patient to drink more water
options.D: Stop the next dose and inform the doctor

explanation: Loss of patellar reflexes is the earliest sign of magnesium toxicity, which means the drug must be paused and the doctor notified immediately. [learn more](BMP124_U3_T6#BMP124_U3_T6_h2)

question: Why must a pregnant woman with epilepsy keep taking her seizure medication?

options.A: To prevent high blood pressure
options.B: To stop morning sickness
options.C: To help the baby's lungs mature early
options.D: To prevent severe, life-threatening seizures

explanation: Stopping epilepsy medication suddenly can cause severe seizures that endanger both the mother and the baby. [learn more](BMP124_U3_T6#BMP124_U3_T6_h3)

question: What usually happens to how the body clears medications as pregnancy progresses?

options.A: Drug clearance stops completely until after birth
options.B: Drug clearance increases because the kidneys work harder
options.C: Drug clearance stays exactly the same
options.D: Drug clearance slows down because the liver rests

explanation: Increased blood flow to the kidneys during pregnancy means drugs are cleared faster, which sometimes requires dose adjustments. [learn more](BMP124_U3_T6#BMP124_U3_T6_h3)

question: Why is folic acid prescribed along with antiepileptic drugs during pregnancy?

options.A: To reduce the risk of neural tube defects
options.B: To speed up brain growth late in pregnancy
options.C: To prevent the mother from developing eclampsia
options.D: To stop bleeding after delivery

explanation: Antiepileptic drugs can interfere with how the body uses folate, so extra folic acid is needed to protect against neural tube abnormalities. [learn more](BMP124_U3_T6#BMP124_U3_T6_h4)

question: What does the word 'teratogenic' mean when talking about medications?

options.A: Causing physical birth defects in a developing baby
options.B: Causing a sudden spike in blood pressure
options.C: Triggers early rupture of membranes
options.D: Stopping contractions during labor

explanation: Teratogenic substances can interfere with normal embryonic or fetal development and cause birth defects. [learn more](BMP124_U3_T6#BMP124_U3_T6_h4)

question: What specific antidote must always be kept nearby when giving magnesium sulphate?

options.A: Calcium gluconate
options.B: Atropine
options.C: Vitamin K
options.D: Naloxone

explanation: Calcium gluconate reverses the effects of magnesium and is used as an emergency antidote if breathing becomes dangerously slow. [learn more](BMP124_U3_T6#BMP124_U3_T6_h5)

question: Which vital sign should a midwife check most often to catch early magnesium toxicity?

options.A: Capillary refill time
options.B: Respiratory rate
options.C: Blood sugar
options.D: Body temperature

explanation: Magnesium toxicity slows down the nervous system, and a falling breathing rate is the key warning sign before more serious complications happen. [learn more](BMP124_U3_T6#BMP124_U3_T6_h5)

question: What is the main goal of selective toxicity when using antimicrobial drugs?

options.A: Preventing the drug from dissolving too quickly
options.B: Boosting the patient's natural immune system response
options.C: Broadening the range of bacteria the drug kills
options.D: Destroying the pathogen without harming host cells

explanation: Selective toxicity means the medication targets and kills the invading germ while keeping the mother's or baby's own cells safe from harm. [learn more](BMP124_U4_T1#BMP124_U4_T1_h1)

question: When should a midwife expect to use empiric antimicrobial therapy?

options.A: Only after all laboratory test results are fully confirmed
options.B: At the very end of a failed course of narrow-spectrum treatment
options.C: When the patient shows an allergy to standard first-line drugs
options.D: Before laboratory culture and sensitivity results are ready

explanation: Empiric treatment starts right away based on clinical signs and common local germs while waiting for lab tests to confirm the exact cause. [learn more](BMP124_U4_T1#BMP124_U4_T1_h1)

question: How do beta-lactamase enzymes protect bacteria from certain drugs?

options.A: By pumping the drug out through special cell wall channels
options.B: By thickening the outer capsule to block drug entry completely
options.C: By breaking down the chemical structure of the medication
options.D: By changing the shape of the internal bacterial ribosomes

explanation: Bacteria that produce beta-lactamase release enzymes that cut the chemical ring of susceptible drugs, making the medication useless against the infection. [learn more](BMP124_U4_T1#BMP124_U4_T1_h2)

question: What happens when bacteria develop active efflux pumps?

options.A: The drug is expelled from the bacterial cell before it can work
options.B: The drug binds permanently to harmless proteins in the bloodstream
options.C: The bacterial cell wall becomes completely impenetrable to water
options.D: The pathogen starts producing its own natural antimicrobial agents

explanation: Efflux pumps act like tiny revolving doors that push entering antimicrobial drugs straight back out before they can cause any damage. [learn more](BMP124_U4_T1#BMP124_U4_T1_h2)

question: Which of the following does NOT drive antimicrobial resistance in the community?

options.A: Purchasing leftover drugs without a professional prescription
options.B: Sharing remaining medications among family members
options.C: Completing the full prescribed dosage of antibiotics
options.D: Using broad-spectrum agents for simple viral infections

explanation: Finishing a prescribed drug course clears the infection completely. Stopping early or misusing drugs is what actually drives resistance. [learn more](BMP124_U4_T1#BMP124_U4_T1_h3)

question: A patient wants to buy strong antibiotics over the counter for a mild cold. What is the main danger of this practice?

options.A: Causing an immediate allergic reaction in the liver tissue
options.B: Promoting drug-resistant strains of bacteria in the community
options.C: Lowering the patient's normal body temperature too quickly
options.D: Killing all beneficial fungi in the upper respiratory tract

explanation: Using antibiotics when they are not needed exposes normal bacteria to the drug, allowing resistant strains to survive, multiply, and spread. [learn more](BMP124_U4_T1#BMP124_U4_T1_h3)

question: What is the main purpose of antimicrobial stewardship programs in healthcare?

options.A: Replacing all injectable medications with oral syrups and tablets
options.B: Promoting the safe, appropriate, and effective use of anti-infective drugs
options.C: Reducing the financial cost of hospital building maintenance and cleaning
options.D: Ensuring that every patient admitted to the ward receives prophylactic drugs

explanation: Stewardship helps ensure drugs are used correctly to get the best clinical results while preventing side effects and slowing down drug resistance. [learn more](BMP124_U4_T1#BMP124_U4_T1_h4)

question: How do basic infection control measures like hand hygiene support antimicrobial stewardship?

options.A: By preventing infections from spreading, reducing the need for drug therapy
options.B: By directly neutralizing resistant bacterial enzymes on the skin surface
options.C: By shortening the time required for laboratory culture results
options.D: By increasing the absorption rate of oral antibiotics in the gut

explanation: Stopping the spread of germs means fewer people get sick in the first place, which naturally cuts down the total number of antibiotics needed. [learn more](BMP124_U4_T1#BMP124_U4_T1_h4)

question: Why is it incorrect to use leftover antibiotics for a new illness later?

options.A: Leftover pills always change color and become toxic to the kidneys
options.B: The leftover drug may be the wrong type and might have lost potency
options.C: Antibiotics always expire within forty-eight hours of opening the bottle
options.D: Using old drugs automatically triggers an immediate anaphylactic shock

explanation: Different illnesses need specific medications. Also, older medications often break down over time and fail to kill bacteria effectively. [learn more](BMP124_U4_T1#BMP124_U4_T1_h5)

question: A postpartum mother says she stopped her prescribed antibiotics after three days because her wound stopped hurting. What is your best response?

options.A: Tell her to double the dose tomorrow to make up for the missed days
options.B: Praise her for saving money and suggest keeping the rest for her baby
options.C: Explain that stopping early leaves strong germs alive and advise completing the dose
options.D: Agree that pain is the only indicator of active bacterial infection

explanation: Midwives teach mothers that feeling better does not mean the infection is fully gone. Stopping early allows stronger bacteria to survive and cause drug resistance. [learn more](BMP124_U4_T1#BMP124_U4_T1_h5)

question: What is the main use of anthelmintic medications?

options.A: To treat infections caused by parasitic worms
options.B: To cure bacterial infections in the bladder
options.C: To prevent viral illnesses like the common cold
options.D: To lower high blood pressure in pregnant women

explanation: Anthelmintics are medications specifically designed to target and clear parasitic worms from the body. [learn more](BMP124_U4_T10#BMP124_U4_T10_h1)

question: Why is treating worm infections especially important for pregnant women?

options.A: Worm burdens interfere with routine ultrasound scans
options.B: Parasites worsen maternal anaemia by stealing vital nutrients
options.C: Helminths directly trigger premature labour contractions
options.D: Worms cause high blood sugar levels during pregnancy

explanation: Worms consume essential nutrients and cause blood loss, which increases the risk of dangerous anaemia during pregnancy. [learn more](BMP124_U4_T10#BMP124_U4_T10_h1)

question: Which parasite is most known for causing iron-deficiency anaemia through intestinal blood loss?

options.A: Tapeworm
options.B: Pinworm
options.C: Hookworm
options.D: Ascaris

explanation: Hookworms attach to the intestinal lining and feed on the host's blood, which leads to iron deficiency. [learn more](BMP124_U4_T10#BMP124_U4_T10_h2)

question: How do people usually catch soil-transmitted worm infections?

options.A: Through mosquito bites during the rainy season
options.B: By walking barefoot on contaminated soil
options.C: By breathing in dust from dry farmland
options.D: Through direct skin contact with infected persons

explanation: Worm larvae in contaminated soil can actively penetrate human skin when individuals walk barefoot. [learn more](BMP124_U4_T10#BMP124_U4_T10_h2)

question: How do drugs like albendazole and mebendazole kill intestinal worms?

options.A: By cutting off the oxygen supply to the worm's lungs
options.B: By blocking glucose uptake and starving the parasite
options.C: By causing immediate relaxation of all worm muscles
options.D: By dissolving the outer protective skin of the worm

explanation: These medications stop worms from absorbing glucose, which starves them of the energy they need to survive. [learn more](BMP124_U4_T10#BMP124_U4_T10_h3)

question: What happens when praziquantel acts on a tapeworm?

options.A: Complete blockage of host digestion
options.B: Spastic paralysis of the parasite
options.C: Rapid multiplication of worm eggs
options.D: Thickening of the worm's outer shell

explanation: Praziquantel causes calcium to flood the worm's cells, leading to sudden muscle contraction and paralysis. [learn more](BMP124_U4_T10#BMP124_U4_T10_h3)

question: During which stage of pregnancy is routine preventive deworming usually delayed?

options.A: Anytime during pregnancy
options.B: Second trimester
options.C: Third trimester
options.D: First trimester

explanation: Routine deworming is withheld during the first trimester to protect early fetal organ development. [learn more](BMP124_U4_T10#BMP124_U4_T10_h4)

question: Why are albendazole or mebendazole given during the second and third trimesters?

options.A: To induce labour safely when a pregnancy reaches full term
options.B: To stop morning sickness and persistent vomiting in late pregnancy
options.C: To reduce maternal anaemia and improve birth outcomes safely
options.D: To completely prevent the mother from ever catching malaria

explanation: Treating worm infections after the first trimester lowers the risk of severe anaemia and supports healthy fetal development. [learn more](BMP124_U4_T10#BMP124_U4_T10_h4)

question: What supplement is usually given alongside routine deworming to help rebuild blood stores?

options.A: Vitamin C and zinc capsules
options.B: Potassium chloride syrups
options.C: Calcium and magnesium tablets
options.D: Iron and folic acid supplements

explanation: Iron and folic acid are given with anti-worm medications to help treat and prevent anaemia caused by blood loss. [learn more](BMP124_U4_T10#BMP124_U4_T10_h5)

question: What is the standard approach when stool tests are not available at a rural antenatal clinic?

options.A: Presumptive treatment based on local endemicity and clinical signs
options.B: Waiting until the patient travels to a city hospital for tests
options.C: Giving multiple strong antibiotics instead of anti-worm drugs
options.D: Withholding all deworming medications until after delivery

explanation: In areas where worms are very common, treating based on clinical guidelines is a safe and accepted public health practice. [learn more](BMP124_U4_T10#BMP124_U4_T10_h5)

question: Which simple habit helps protect individuals from catching hookworm infections?

options.A: Wearing protective footwear outdoors
options.B: Avoiding all contact with sunlight
options.C: Sleeping under insecticide nets
options.D: Boiling all drinking water twice

explanation: Since hookworm larvae live in damp soil and penetrate bare skin, wearing shoes acts as an important barrier. [learn more](BMP124_U4_T10#BMP124_U4_T10_h6)

question: Why is health education on handwashing and sanitation important alongside deworming?

options.A: To prevent reinfection after the current worms are cleared
options.B: To stop pregnant women from developing gestational diabetes
options.C: To cure existing malaria infections concurrently
options.D: To make the deworming tablets dissolve faster in the stomach

explanation: Good hygiene and sanitation stop patients from picking up new worm infections from their environment after treatment. [learn more](BMP124_U4_T10#BMP124_U4_T10_h6)

question: What type of germs do antiprotozoal drugs specifically target?

options.A: Rapidly mutating viral particles
